where: Section 1, first paragraph of the derivation
problem: The sentence 'The pressure head the pump must produce is the manometric head Hm' calls Hm a pressure head. The manometric head is a total head in metres; it contains the pressure rise, the velocity head difference and the elevation difference. Calling it a pressure head can make a student read Hm as p/(ρg) only.
fix: The head the pump must produce is the manometric head Hm, expressed in metres of the pumped liquid.

problem: 'At standstill the impeller cannot push water into a delivery pipe that already needs a pressure head' mixes up standstill with low speed. At standstill the impeller gives no head at all; the argument is about speeds below Nmin, where the head exists but is smaller than Hm.
fix: At low speed the impeller head is smaller than the manometric head needed by the delivery pipe, so no water is pushed into it. The head falls to zero only when the impeller stops.

problem: The note does not say which operating point eta_man belongs to. At shut-off the useful hydraulic power is zero, so the efficiency there is zero, and a student may wonder why a non-zero eta_man is put into the formula.
fix: Add: eta_man is the manometric efficiency at the normal duty point of the pump; use that value as a fixed input in the formula.

problem: The closing claim 'flow increases by less than double' is only true when pipe friction dominates the system curve. If the system is mostly static head (a deep borewell lift, for example), doubling the head can more than double the flow, so a student can carry away a wrong general rule.
fix: Series doubles the head at a given Q, not the flow. The new duty point is where the doubled pump curve meets the system curve, so the flow rise depends on the system: less than double when friction (rises as Q squared) dominates, more than double when a large static head dominates.
